artifact.self_contained_problem:
Let $(M,g)$ be a smooth Riemannian (or pseudo-Riemannian) manifold of dimension $n \geq 3$, and let $V \colon M \to \mathbb{R}$ be a smooth potential. Consider the natural Hamiltonian system on the cotangent bundle $T^*M$ with Hamiltonian
$$H(q,p) \;=\; \tfrac{1}{2}\, g^{ij}(q)\, p_i p_j \;+\; V(q),$$
where $(q,p)$ are canonical coordinates on $T^*M$. A function $F \colon T^*M \to \mathbb{R}$ is called polynomial in momenta of degree $d$ if, in any canonical chart,
$$F(q,p) \;=\; \sum_{|\alpha|\le d} a_\alpha(q)\, p^\alpha$$
with smooth coefficients $a_\alpha$. The system $(M,g,V)$ is said to be Liouville integrable in the class of integrals polynomial in momenta if there exist $n$ functions $F_1=H, F_2,\ldots,F_n$ on $T^*M$, each polynomial in momenta, that are functionally independent almost everywhere and pairwise Poisson-commuting: $\{F_i,F_j\}=0$.

Problem: Construct new explicit examples of natural Hamiltonian systems $(M,g,V)$ with $\dim M \geq 3$ that are Liouville integrable in this class of integrals polynomial in momenta and are not equivalent (by isometry, scaling, or reduction) to known examples. In particular, investigate whether new integrable natural systems can be produced in the setting of Lorentzian metrics arising in General Relativity, beyond the geodesic integrability of the Schwarzschild and Kerr metrics, by adjoining nontrivial potentials $V$ while preserving the existence of a complete set of polynomial-in-momenta first integrals.
artifact.status_search_result: The question is posed as a research direction asking for the construction of new examples rather than as a single conjecture to prove or disprove. While many classes of integrable natural Hamiltonian systems with polynomial integrals are known in dimension 2 and some in higher dimensions, the construction of new higher-dimensional examples (and integrable extensions of relativistic metrics like Schwarzschild/Kerr with potential) remains an active area of research with no definitive resolution. Status is best described as open/ongoing.
